NPU Compilation Optimization

What dominates Intel NPU-5 compile time, why, and what to fix — 133 cold configs over 5 architecture families (Gemma-2, TinyLlama, Llama-3.2, Phi-3, Qwen2), sizes 0.5–14.8 B, prompt window 128 → 32768, three weight precisions (int4 / int8 / fp16), 10 cold repeats each (OpenVINO 2026.0).

The dominant pass is not fixed by architecture — it's set by how big the compile is. Every family walks the same path: tiling-search → memory-scheduling → serialization. And each pass's cost tracks the IR/schedule size it processes — which is the handle to fix it.

2 · The handoff is universal across architectures

3 · Why those passes are costly — cost = f(IR/schedule size)

4 · Same fingerprint, different architectures

5 · Precision: a two-way tug-of-war, not "fewer bits = faster"

Compile cost is a tug-of-war between two effects. The dequantization / weight-table machinery that int8 and int4 bolt on penalises the quantized formats — so for small-to-mid models fp16 compiles fastest (≈0.58× int8) despite its larger weights. But fp16 also carries 2× the weight bytes, and by 7 B that weight-DMA volume takes over: fp16 flips to ≈0.87× int8 (up to 2.4× at mid windows). int4 wins both ways — it has the dequant machinery but half the bytes — staying ≤0.99× int8 at every size. Modal dominant stage by precision: int4→memory-scheduling, int8→serialization, fp16→tiling-search.

6 · Convolutional graphs — same structure, different passes

The pattern generalises across modality, with a twist. Across 31 CNN configs (7 families — ResNet-18→152 swept 128→640 px, plus EfficientNet, MobileNetV3, DenseNet, RegNet, Inception, ConvNeXt), FeasibleAllocation never dominates a single compile (0/31). Conv graphs are tiling + vertical-fusion bound: MultiClusterStrategy (tiling) leads at low resolution and hands off to MergeVfSubgraphs (vertical fusion) as resolution grows. Same workload-gated shape as the LLMs — attention graphs escalate into scheduling/serialization; conv graphs escalate into tiling/fusion.

7 · Testing a lever: what happens if the compiler stops prefetching

The levers above are hypotheses until one is measured. prefetching is a single pipeline option gating both the prefetch tiling search and the FeasibleAllocation prefetch scheduler, so it is the one lever that can be switched with a property rather than a patch: NPU_COMPILATION_MODE_PARAMS="prefetching=false". Two arms per cell, compiled back-to-back, then inferred in the same process so the latency belongs to the blob whose compile was just timed.

The compile saving is large and unconditional — 6–54% (up to 227s off a single 7B compile). The inference cost is not: its sign flips with model size. 0.5B, 1.8B pay for it; 3.1B, 7.6B, 14.8B get faster decode as well — up to 15% per token. For prefill the flip has a threshold: prefetching only starts paying once the window is long enough to hold compute to hide movement behind (3.1B at W=1024, 7.6B at W=4096) — and that threshold rises with model size.

Where the compile saving actually comes from

Mostly not from one pass. Below 7.6B no single pass accounts for more than 6% of the saving — it is spread across nearly the whole pipeline, and per-pass timings account for 94–97% of the wall-clock saving, so this is not unmeasured overhead. The exception is 7.6B, where FeasibleAllocation alone gives back 17s (4%) — that is the CMX scheduler falling out of the regime §3 identifies. Tiling search, the other thing the flag gates, is never more than 6%.

The reason nearly every pass gets cheaper at once is visible in the last column: the pipeline is identical (3794 pass invocations either way) but the schedule it processes is 25–49% smaller. Prefetching does not move more data — it splits the same work into many more, smaller tasks so they can be issued early. Every downstream pass then walks a bigger task graph.

1.8B248s7s (3%)10s (4%)Canonicalizer 6%, StaticAllocation 3%, ConvertVPUMI40XX2VPUASM 3%-25%

Why decode gets faster on the big models

Not because less data moves. On the decode graph — the one re-executed for every generated token — the work is almost unchanged when prefetching is off: DMA work -2 to -7% and DPU work about −7%. What collapses is the number of scheduled tasks. Prefetching splits the same transfers into many more, smaller ones so they can be issued early, and removing it cuts the decode task graph by 29–54% at 3.1B/7.6B against only 18–19% at 0.5B/1.8B. Every task carries fixed cost the cycle model never charges for — barrier programming, descriptor fetch, DMA setup — so the big models shed enough per-task overhead to more than pay back the lost overlap, and the small models do not. That is the sign flip.

The compiler's own model gets it backwards: it predicts decode should get slower by about +1.8% for every size. It is right in sign for 0.5B/1.8B and wrong for 3.1B/7.6B, because it prices work and overlap but not the cost of having more tasks to run.

modeldecode tasksDMA workDPU work modelled makespanmeasured decode
0.5B-19%-1.7%-1.5%+1.1%+3.0%
1.8B-18%-2.2%-6.4%+2.6%+4.0%
3.1B-54%-7.4%-6.8%+3.7%-10.1%
7.6B-39%-2.9%-6.9%+1.8%-14.3%
14.8B-29%-2.1%-5.2%-6.9%-1.9%

It does not keep scaling with size. The decode win peaks at 7.6B (-14%) and falls back to -1.9% at 14.8B — and the task-graph reduction that drives it falls with it: turning prefetch off removes 38% of the scheduled tasks at 7.6B but only 17% at 14.8B. Reading the 7.6B result as "bigger model, bigger win" would be wrong: prefetching inflates the 14.8B task graph far less, so switching it off frees far less. The mechanism predicts the reversal that the size trend alone does not.

Control — is the big-model speedup an artifact?

A result that says "do less scheduling, go faster" deserves suspicion, so the sweep's design was attacked directly. In the sweep, prefetch-on always compiled first inside a cell and each arm was measured in its own process, so a warmed device or thermal drift could have produced the gap. The control removes both: it compiles both arms in one process with the order reversed (off first), then measures decode by alternating between them over six rounds, alternating which arm leads each round. It also compares the two blobs' prefill logits on identical input — a blob that is faster because it computes something different would be a bug, not a speedup.

modelwindowdecode, prefetch ondecode, prefetch off deltaworst spreadoutput vs the other arm
3.1BW=20481,381 ms1,238 ms-10.4%3 msbit-identical
7.6BW=20483,072 ms2,624 ms-14.6%40 msbit-identical
14.8BW=20488,879 ms8,699 ms-2.0%14 msbit-identical

The gap survives unchanged — the control reproduces the sweep to within a few tenths of a percent — and where the logits were compared the two arms are bit-identical. The effect is neither an ordering artifact nor a correctness regression.

Read this narrowly. prefetching is global — it gates the tiling search as well as the allocator, so this is the prefetch feature, not the allocator in isolation; separating them would need a patched compiler. The overlap/DMA-work numbers are the compiler's modelled schedule, not hardware counters: per-op runtime profiling is unavailable through NPUW (get_profiling_info() returns empty), which is itself part of the finding — the only per-op view available is the model that turns out to mispredict. 4 of 42 cells (0.5B@W=128, 0.5B@W=512, 0.5B@W=4096, 0.5B@W=8192) are unresolved — their arm-to-arm decode difference is smaller than the spread within an arm (up to 90.8 ms on a ~130 ms decode), so they carry no direction and are excluded from the decode ranges quoted here. All four are 0.5B: the smallest model is the one whose decode effect is the same size as its run-to-run noise.

8 · Inside FeasibleAllocation — a CPU flame graph

§3 says this pass dominates 7B compiles and §7 says turning its prefetching off gives most of that time back. Neither says what it is doing. This is a perf profile of a cold Qwen2.5-7B INT8 compile at window 2048, on the from-source compiler relinked with its symbol table intact. The pass's own timer reports 17.2% of wall clock against 19.4% of CPU cycles — the two agree, so the pass is genuinely doing work rather than waiting.

Nearly half of it is sorting. msort_with_tmp plus llvm::array_pod_sort_comparator<unsigned long> account for 49% of the pass's cycles, reached through vpux::AsyncDepsInfo::getDepsVec (12% self time), with another 9% in memmove shuffling the results. The call path the graph shows is safeRunOnFunc → PrefetchDataOps::prefetchDataOps → AsyncDepsInfo::getOpDeps → getDepsVec → qsort_r → msort_with_tmp: the dependency vector is re-sorted, repeatedly, while the scheduler walks the graph. That is a data-structure problem, not an algorithmic one — which makes it a far more tractable target than "the scheduler is slow".

Two corrections to an earlier version of this section. It reported the pass at 7.4% of CPU against 17.2% of wall and concluded it was "wall-heavy and CPU-light — serialization, not computation". That was wrong. The cause was stackcollapse-perf.pl: it extracts the trailing (dso) with a pattern that stops at the first ( on the line, so every demangled C++ name with a parameter list was cut there, which broke both symbol matching and stack structure. With a collapser that anchors the dso to the end of the line, CPU and wall agree and the serialization claim disappears. The same fix cut the unresolvable share from 56% to 7%. Those remaining stacks are still marked "⚠ unwind truncated" rather than drawn as if their depth were measured — the library is built -O3 without frame pointers, so perf cannot always unwind it.

9 · The sort in FeasibleAllocation — what it costs, and an order-preserving cache

§8 profiled this pass and found its heaviest frames were a sort, reached through vpux::AsyncDepsInfo::getDepsVec. That was an inference from a profile. This section patches the compiler and measures: how much time is that sort worth, and what does taking it back cost you? The short answer is 15% of total compile time while preserving dependency order and tested output quality. The trade-off is cache storage plus correct invalidation whenever a task's dependencies change.

Step 1 — what the function does

Every task in the scheduler's graph (an async.execute op) has a set of other tasks it must wait for. getDepsVec takes one such set, copies it out of a DenseSet into a vector, sorts it, and returns it. The sort is not decoration — the comment says the order feeds the DMA prefetch order:

SmallVector<size_t> vpux::AsyncDepsInfo::getDepsVec(const llvm::DenseSet<size_t>& deps) const {
    SmallVector<size_t> vec(deps.begin(), deps.end());
    /* The order of dependencies may impact order of prefetched DMA.
     * Experiments show that arbitrary order of these dependencies may impact
     * inference accuracy (E102917) hence sorting.
     */
    llvm::sort(vec.begin(), vec.end());
    return vec;
}

Remember that comment — it defines the whole section. A change that keeps the order identical asks the scheduler for the same decisions, so it emits the same program and cannot affect accuracy. A change that alters the order emits a different program, and then accuracy has to be measured rather than argued.

Step 2 — how much work is that, really?

Counters compiled into the function, one cold Qwen2.5-7B INT8 compile at window 2048:

70% of calls carry more than 16 entries, so this is a real sorting workload rather than a few trivial ones.

The sorting number is a union: a sampled stack containing qsort_r, msort_with_tmp, or LLVM's POD-sort comparator counts once, so nested frames are not double-counted. The graph's shape is unchanged by this linear normalisation; its absolute labels now answer the per-call question. Memoisation's −14.17% remains the causal wall-clock A/B result. It avoids repeated DenseSet-to-vector materialisation, sorting, qsort temporary allocation, and indirect comparisons; the cached SmallVector is still returned by value. CPU seconds sum concurrent threads and therefore are not subtracted directly from wall seconds. The profile uses the retained symbol-rich stock compiler from the same base commit as the mode-selectable A/B build; its build ID is checked against perf.data before this graph is generated.

Step 5 — two candidate explanations

(a) The sort primitive is slow. llvm::sort reads like an ordinary fast C++ sort, but for plain copyable values like integers it forwards to llvm::array_pod_sort, which calls the C library's qsort. std::sort is a template, so the comparison inlines into the loop; qsort takes a pointer to a comparison function, so every comparison is an indirect call that cannot be inlined, and glibc's qsort is a merge sort that allocates a temporary buffer per call. LLVM chose this deliberately, to avoid instantiating a sort template per type, and its comment states the assumption behind the trade:

/// array_pod_sort - ... it calls qsort instead of using an inlined template.
/// qsort is slightly slower than std::sort, but most sorts are not performance
/// critical in LLVM and std::sort has to be template instantiated for each
/// type, leading to significant measured code bloat.

That assumption is reasonable in general and wrong in this one place: this sort is on the hot path of the pass that dominates 7B compiles. (Verified in the object file, not just the header — getDepsVec is the only function in its translation unit referencing qsort@PLT.)

(b) The work is redundant. The scheduler walks the graph repeatedly, asking for the same task's dependencies over and over. If the set has not changed since last time, re-copying and re-sorting it is wasted.

These predict different fixes, so both were built.

Step 6 — the patches

All arms are the same binary; the strategy is picked by an environment variable, so nothing differs between them but the one decision.

armwhat it changeskeeps dependency order?
memoiseCache the sorted vector per task; recompute only when that task's dependencies actually change.yes
std::sortReplace llvm::sort with std::sort, so the comparison inlines instead of going through a function pointer.yes
memoise + std::sortBoth of the above.yes
delete the sortReturn the dependency set unsorted.no
prefetching=falseTurn the whole prefetch feature off (§7's lever), which removes most of the calls at their source.no

Step 8 — redundancy wins, by 3×

Explanation (b) is the dominant one. Memoising is worth up to 15.4% of total compile time; fixing the primitive across all 1.8 billion elements is worth only 6.2%. The counters say why: the cache answers 95.6% of lookups, cutting calls by 94% and elements by 99%. Doing both (15.5%) adds nothing over memoising alone — once 94% of the calls are gone, which sort you use stops mattering.

Step 9 — is it a cache-locality problem? No.

A third explanation is worth testing explicitly: "copying out of a hash set 33 million times" sounds like a cache problem. std::sort receives the same vectors and elements as stock, but uses an in-place introsort where glibc qsort uses temporary merge buffers, so it is a useful primitive comparison rather than a claim of identical memory touches. Memoising keeps the ordering rule while reducing dependency elements rematerialised and sorted by 99.1% (1.85 billion elements down to 16.5 million).

counter (vs stock)std::sortmemoisedcounted on
cycles-9.7%-13.8%both
instructions-11.2%-12.2%both
cache-misses-4.1%-3.3%both
LLC-load-misses-9.3%-13.6%E-cores only
L1-dcache-load-misses-0.8%+1.3%P-cores only
dTLB-load-misses-4.1%-2.2%both

Processing 99.1% fewer dependency elements moved total cache misses by only 3.3% — and P-core L1 misses went slightly up. That is much smaller than the reduction in elements and argues against cache misses being the dominant cost. What moved instead is instruction count: cycles −13.8% tracking instructions −12.2%, with IPC essentially unchanged (~2.2 on the P-cores in both arms). The cost is primarily instruction retirement, not memory stalls — work over 1.85 billion dependency elements driven through an out-of-line qsort with an indirect comparator. Memoising wins by not executing them, not by making them hit cache.

hybrid CPU: LLC-load-misses counted on E-core PMU only, L1-dcache-load-misses on P-core PMU only; cache-misses counted on both. Partial-coverage rows are labelled rather than presented as machine-wide; cache-misses, the row carrying the argument, counted on both PMUs.

Step 10 — does any of it cost accuracy?

Step 1 predicts the three order-preserving arms cannot change the model, and leaves the other two open — the E102917 comment exists precisely because reordering might matter. Every arm was scored on 500 ARC-Easy questions, greedy, one forward pass each, and compared to stock answer by answer.

armARC-Easyaccuracyvs stock, question by question
stock459/50091.8%all 500 identical
prefetching=false459/50091.8%all 500 identical
delete the sort459/50091.8%all 500 identical
memoise459/50091.8%all 500 identical
std::sort459/50091.8%all 500 identical
memoise + std::sort459/50091.8%all 500 identical

The order-preserving arms come back identical, as predicted — which is also a check that the cache invalidation is correct, since a stale entry would have shown up here. The two reordering arms come back identical too, so E102917's warning did not reproduce on this workload. That is a weaker claim than it looks: see the limits below.

Step 11 — what to do

  1. Memoise getDepsVec, invalidated on addDependency. ~15% of compile time, order-preserving, roughly ten lines.
  2. Return ArrayRef instead of a by-value SmallVector, removing the copy §8 measured at ~9% of the pass.
  3. Store _depsMap sorted rather than as a DenseSet, which removes the copy-and-sort entirely.
  4. Use std::sort — ~6%, one line, but the smallest of the four.

Turning prefetching off entirely remains larger at 39%; §7 covers what that costs at inference time.

Limits of these claims

The accuracy result is prefill-only. ARC scores one forward pass per question, so it does not exercise long decode chains, where a DMA-ordering effect would have the most room to accumulate. GSM8K was meant to cover that and currently dies mid-decode on the 7B, so the E102917 question is open for generation even though it is settled for prefill. This is also why the recommendation is memoisation and not deleting the sort: the memo does not need the question answered.

The blob hash is not an equivalence test, and was nearly used as one. The order-preserving arms should emit a byte-identical blob, and on a plain-static ResNet-50 they do — but under NPUW_LLM neither do two stock compiles of the same model at the same window (6e958e5354f4 vs fe405d709f96). Serialisation is not reproducible run-to-run, so a mismatch proves nothing. Hashes are provenance here; the table above is the evidence.

delete the sort is not a controlled comparison. It scores as well as the memo, but it is solving a different problem: with the order changed the scheduler makes different decisions, and the counters move with it — 15,106,679 calls instead of 33,334,741. Part of its saving is a smaller graph, not cheaper work. The memo is the controlled arm, and it lands at the same number.

10 · The fixable pattern → what to optimize

Because cost is driven by IR/schedule size in a known regime, the levers are direct:

regime (when)dominant passroot causefix
every compile—recompiling from scratch Warm blob cache — a recompile is 20–30× a blob-load. Biggest, universal win.
small / short (≤3B)MultiClusterStrategy serial tiling search (user/wall≈1.0) Cache / reuse strategy_out.json across shapes; lower search effort.
7B, mid windowFeasibleAllocation #tasks explodes → greedy simulate-and-spill re-run 2–3× Fewer/larger tiles (cut #tasks); bound the window; ship precompiled ELF.
≥3B, any windowMultiClusterStrategy
+ FeasibleAllocation		 prefetch tiling + prefetch scheduling search Turn prefetching off (prefetching=false) — measured in §7: 53% off the compile at best and 9–14% faster decode at 3B/7B. Below 3B it costs latency; above it, it is free both ways.
extreme window (≥16K)ELF serialization artifact size grows linearly with W Precompiled-blob shipping; the materialization is mechanical, don't repeat it.

Method: Intel Core Ultra 7 356H, NPU 5 (intel_vpu), OpenVINO 2026.0, driver-compiler 1.33. Weights swept at int4 (symmetric, group-128), int8 and fp16 — each export's on-disk element types verified (fp16 defeats the optimum silent-int8 trap; int4 uses --sym to dodge a group-quant location-verifier compiler bug that fails asymmetric int4). Fully-cold compiles (NPU_BYPASS_UMD_CACHING, isolated subprocess per repeat), NPUW_LLM window sweep. Per-pass time = the VPUX compiler's MLIR PassTiming (wall, inclusive of analyses, pipeline groups excluded); mean over 10 repeats (4 at W≥8192). Why-costly metrics from the release compiler's own instrumentation via NPU_COMPILATION_MODE_PARAMS (enable-schedule-trace, write-strategy-to-json) + built-in dump-statistics-of-ie-ops. The §3 FeasibleAllocation-knee figure is measured on a from-source build of the open npu_compiler (compiler-in-plugin, commit 30d2bb8, OpenVINO 2026.2) — the same MLIR passes run in-process on the schedulable compiler, cold, 2 repeats, window 128→32768. Sparse-MoE (Granite) and hybrid-SSM (Qwen3.5) do not compile on NPU 5 (dynamic shapes). CNNs exported via optimum --library timm, reshaped to static NCHW; input resolution is the plain-static workload axis. vgg16 excluded — its 102M-param fc1 fails SplitNCEOpsOntoWorkloads on NPU 5. Ungated model mirrors; no HF token.
